note: Korean names in Latin letters (#93): the same name is written in the South's Revised Romanization (Jeong Eun), McCune-Reischauer (Chŏng Ŭn, diacritics and apostrophes already gone: Chong Un), the North's own spelling (Jong Un) and popular spellings (Chung, Lee, Park). A name of two to four words, each one or two syllables these spellings can make (or a surname's spelling), with a surname from 'surnames' first or last, is read as Korean: each word gets a reading per way its syllables can be split, from the classes below (an initial, a vowel, a final), so spellings of one syllable read alike. 'initials', 'vowels' and 'finals' give each spelling its class; an initial r or n before i or y, which the South drops (Ri, Yi; Ryong, Yong), also reads without it, and an initial r otherwise as n (Ro, No). Popular spellings write eo as u (Sung, Hyun, Chul), so o and u are one class. 'surnames' are the spellings of each common surname, for the ones the classes don't join (Lee, Park, Choi, Ahn). Read by the Rust port only; .NET and Go hash it.
